card: Paper card. Question: What are the atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the exceptional damage tolerance (high strength, ductility, and fracture toughness) of the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy?. System: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (single-phase fcc solid solution). Processing: Arc-melting high-purity elemental starting materials, drop casting into copper moulds, cold forging and cross rolling at room temperature, recrystallization at 800 °C (grain size ∼6 μm), followed by ion milling (5 kV) or twin jet polishing (10 °C, 13 mA/12 V) to create electron-transparent foils with cracks. Test conditions: In situ straining in an aberration-corrected TEM (FEI Tecnai G2 F20, 200 kV) at room temperature using pulsed tensile loading (axial displacement rate ∼1.0 μm s⁻¹). Findings: Early deformation is dominated by the easy motion of Shockley partial dislocations (1/6<112> type) and the continuous nucleation/annihilation of stacking faults (SFs).; Interactions between partials on different {111} planes form stable 'stacking-fault parallelepipeds' (volume defects) that act as formidable obstacles for dislocation motion.; Perfect (undissociated, 1/2<110> type) dislocations move with extreme difficulty in localized bands of planar slip, creating strong barriers that arrest fast-moving partial dislocations.; The motion of perfect dislocations requires overcoming continuous activation barriers, indicative of high friction stress in the alloy.; Nanoscale voids form in the 'semi-cohesive zone' at the intersection of two {111} slip planes, creating fiber-like bridges spanning the crack faces.; These nanobridges (size <200 nm, some ∼100 nm) deform primarily via nano-twinning ({111} twin structure), which accommodates strain and shields the crack tip.; The synergy of these mechanisms yields tensile strength ∼1 GPa, ductility ∼60–70%, and fracture toughness K_JIc > 200 MPa√m.. Mechanism: The authors propose a synergistic sequence where intrinsic toughening arises from easy partial dislocation motion (ductility) followed by strain hardening via stacking-fault parallelepipeds and planar slip bands (strength). Extrinsic toughening occurs via nanoscale twinned bridges that form behind the crack tip, carrying load and shielding the crack tip from the applied driving force.. Limitations: The study notes that 'ultrahigh-resolution observations have to be made at the nanoscale to permit any characterization of mechanisms so close to the crack tip,' and that 'thin foil samples must be used which, under load, cannot display the full constraint of a bulk sample.'. Future work: The authors state that 'further optimization of these mechanisms may present new directions for the future design of advanced metallic materials with unprecedented damage tolerance.'. Quote: "We identify a synergy of multiple deformation mechanisms, rarely achieved in metallic alloys, which generates high strength, work hardening and ductility"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility trade-off inherent to traditional alloys be overcome in multi-principal-element alloys by exploiting multiple levels of heterogeneities?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) and medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) including FCC-based systems (e.g., CoCrFeNi, CrCoNi, VCoNi), BCC-based refractory systems (e.g., TiZrHfNbTa), dual-phase eutectic lamella HEAs, and alloys with multicomponent intermetallic nanoparticles (MCINPs). Processing: Partial recrystallization to create heterogeneous grain structures (HGS), spinodal decomposition to form precipitates, addition of oxygen solutes (~2 at%) to form nanoscale complexes, and intentional alloying to tune stacking fault energy (SFE) for deformation-induced transformations. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) uniaxial tensile testing; cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K) for specific FCC MEAs; compression testing for some refractory BCC HEAs. Findings: An FCC-MCINP alloy achieved a yield strength above 1 GPa with a uniform elongation (εu) of ~50%, showing no strength–ductility trade-off compared to unstrengthened elemental metals.; A single-phase CrCoNi MEA with a heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nano-to-micro scales reached a gigapascal yield strength while maintaining εu in excess of 20%.; The VCoNi MEA achieved near-GPa yield strength with εu ~30% and total elongation ~38%, attributed to maximized lattice friction from atomic size mismatch.; In BCC-TiZrHfNb HEA, adding ~2 at% oxygen formed nanoscale (O, Ti, Zr)-complexes that increased tensile elongation from ~14% to ~28% while maintaining high strength.; Stress-assisted martensitic transformation in BCC-Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 HEA created a 65% volume fraction of internally twinned martensite, doubling the strain-hardening rate.; Wide hysteresis loops in load–unload–reload stress–strain curves demonstrated that nonhomogeneous plastic deformation in HGS alloys imparts high back stresses contributing to strain hardening.; At cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K), the CrCoNi MEA exhibited strain-hardening rates and εu comparable to the best 316 austenitic stainless steels due to reduced dynamic recovery.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high concentration of multiple principal elements creates a rugged energy landscape with statistical fluctuations in composition and local chemical order (LCO), causing dislocations to adopt a wavy line and face intermittent 'nanoscale segment detrapping' barriers. This intrinsic lattice friction is compounded by a hierarchy of heterogeneities (defects, precipitates, grain boundaries, phase boundaries) that promote nonhomogeneous plastic deformation, geometrically necessary dislocation storage, and dynamic mechanisms like twinning (TWIP) and transformation (TRIP), which sustain high strain-hardening rates to delay necking.. Limitations: Refractory BCC HEAs often lack room-temperature tensile ductility due to a drastic rise in the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature; TRIP-assisted DP alloys with low initial yield strength require hardening (e.g., cold work) which causes the strain-hardening rate to become inadequate, restoring the strength–ductility trade-off at high σy levels.. W2554394793.title: Directly cast bulk eutectic and near-eutectic high entropy alloys with balanced strength and ductility in a wide temperature range

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility synergy in eutectic high-entropy alloys be improved by inheriting the composite lamellar nature through tailored thermo-mechanical processing?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (at%) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Arc-melting followed by suction-casting into a copper mold, multi-pass cold-rolling to 84–86% reduction in thickness, and non-isothermal annealing at 660, 700, 740, or 900 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests with an initial strain rate of 2.5 × 10−4 s−1 using dog-bone specimens (15 mm gauge length, 3.2 mm width, 600 μm thickness) and loading–unloading–reloading (LUR) tests.. Findings: The DPHL700 and DPHL740 samples achieved a yield strength of approximately 1.5 GPa with an elongation of ~16%, representing a simultaneous enhancement in both strength and ductility compared to as-cast and ultrafine-grained counterparts.; The microstructure exhibited a two-hierarchical heterogeneity consisting of submicron-grade FCC/B2 grains within FCC lamellae and micron-grade alternate FCC/B2 lamellae.; The average diameters of FCC and B2 grains were roughly comparable at ~0.71 μm, with inter-lamella spacings ranging from 1.5 to 5 μm.; Phase decomposition resulted in two types of NiAl-rich precipitates in FCC lamellae: small intragranular P1 grains (50–180 nm) and large intergranular P2 grains (~350 nm).; Back-stress measurements at the yield point reached ~950 MPa, which was approximately 3 times higher than the effective stress, primarily responsible for the high yield strength.; The strain-hardening rate (Θ) showed a transient behavior with an up-turn in region II and sustained high Θ over a wide strain region III for DPHL700.; Microcrack-arresting mechanisms were observed where multiple microcracks were inhibited from coalescing, with ductile components acting as efficient crack arresters.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced properties to a two-hierarchical constraint effect that generates long-range back-stress by storing geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) due to strain gradients at lamella interfaces and around intergranular precipitates, combined with a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism where the aligned lamellar architecture delays crack propagation and coalescence.. Limitations: The authors note that while the DPHL structure is effective, increasing the annealing temperature to 900 °C induced a partially degraded lamellar structure that led to inferior tensile properties, indicating the sensitivity of the process to thermal treatment.. Future work: The authors propose that further efforts should be devoted to exploring non-equiatomic alloys and spinodal decomposition to create low-misfit coherent nanostructures for even higher yield strengths, and anticipate modifying the EHEA to satisfy requirements for high-temperature and/or corrosion environments.. Quote: "The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the capacity for twinning-controlled deformation in the equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy generate a simultaneous increase in strength and ductility, and what is the origin of its exceptional fracture toughness?. System: Nominally equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a single-phase face-centered cubic (fcc) structure. Processing: Samples extracted from a previously produced alloy; micro-pillars (~300 nm diameter) machined using focused-ion beam (FIB) techniques; in situ TEM compression tests performed at 300 kV; in situ TEM tensile tests conducted at room temperature using a Gatan model 654 single-tilt straining holder at 200 kV; DFT calculations performed using VASP with the nudged-elastic band method. Test conditions: Room temperature (300 K); uniaxial tension and compression; micro-pillar compression at 300 kV; in situ straining at 10 frames per second; DFT calculations at 0 K and 500 K. Findings: The alloy exhibits high strength (~1 GPa), ductility (~60% uniform elongation), and exceptional fracture toughness (KIc > 200 MPa√m).; Ab initio calculations reveal a negative intrinsic stacking-fault energy (γisf = −23 mJ m−2) at 0 K and a high twinnability value (τta = 1.07 ± 0.02).; Deformation activates three twinning systems within individual coarse grains (5–50 μm), forming a stable 3D hierarchical twin network with twin thicknesses ranging from ~100 nm to several micrometres.; Micro-pillars containing a pre-existing {111} twin boundary showed a maximum strength exceeding 2.5 GPa, approximately 1 GPa higher than pillars without a twin.; Dislocations pile up at coherent twin boundaries (CTBs), acting as strong barriers to motion, while intersecting twin boundaries serve as fast channels for dislocation glide.; Dislocations cross-slip between intersecting twin boundaries via an 'overpass' mechanism, enabling homogeneous plastic deformation in three dimensions.; The 3D twin architecture remains stable during deformation with no evidence of twin growth or de-twinning, even as dislocations move rapidly along the boundaries.. Mechanism: The 3D hierarchical twin network provides a dual function: conventional strengthening occurs via the blockage of dislocations impinging on twin boundaries, while the interconnected network offers pathways for dislocation glide along and cross-slip between intersecting twin-matrix interfaces, allowing simultaneous high strength and ductility.. Limitations: The study notes that nano-pillar tests investigate limited volumes; detailed processes of sessile dislocation involvement in cross-slip were not fully captured due to limited time-resolution of in situ TEM; the specific role of magnetization was analyzed but calculations were mainly performed on non-magnetic structures.. Future work: The authors propose that documenting this enhanced twinning-induced toughness may present new directions for the future design of metallic alloys with unprecedented combinations of mechanical properties.. Quote: "This serves a dual function: conventional twin-boundary (TB) strengthening from blockage of dislocations impinging on TBs, coupled with the 3D twin network which offers pathways for dislocation glide along, and cross-slip between, intersecting TB-matrix interfaces."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the stability of austenite in Fe-Mn-Al duplex lightweight steels be optimized to achieve a combination of high tensile strength and high ductility without the steady flow behavior (plastic instability) observed in previous (TRIP+TWIP) steels?. System: Fe-0.3C-9Mn-5Al (modified) and Fe-0.3C-8.5Mn-5.6Al (previous) duplex lightweight steels; annealed variants A850, A900, A950. Processing: Vacuum induction melting; homogenization at 1200 °C for 1 hour; hot-rolling between 1100 °C and 900 °C; furnace cooling from 650 °C; cold rolling to 1 mm; annealing at 850, 900, or 950 °C for 5 min; cooling to 400 °C at -14 °C s⁻¹ followed by air cooling. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹ using ASTM E 8/E 8 M standard specimens (gage length 25 mm, width 6 mm, thickness 1 mm). Findings: The modified Fe-0.3C-9Mn-5Al steel annealed at 900 °C (A900) achieved a tensile strength of 874 MPa and elongation of 72%.; The A850 steel (annealed at 850 °C) exhibited an elongation of 95% with a tensile strength of 785 MPa.; The A900 steel showed the highest true tensile strength of 1496 MPa among the annealed variants.; The A950 steel (annealed at 950 °C) showed an abrupt reduction in elongation to about 25% despite a tensile strength of 840 MPa.; In the A900 steel, the volume fraction of martensite increased by 30% from Stage B to failure, compared to 15% in the A850 steel.; Plastic instability did not occur in the A900 steel until failure because the strain hardening rate remained considerably higher than the true stress.; The austenite fraction in the modified steel was 56% after 66%-cold-rolling and annealing at 900 °C for 30 min.; The austenite grain size in the A900 steel was 2.1 μm, compared to 1.7 μm in A850 and 2.6 μm in A950.. Mechanism: The authors argue that decreasing austenite stability (indirectly via increased austenite fraction and alloying partitioning) promotes a dominant TRIP mechanism over TWIP in the A900 steel. This active TRIP, occurring at lower critical strains with higher rates, generates a high strain hardening rate that delays plastic instability. In contrast, the A850 steel retains high stability leading to simultaneous TRIP and TWIP, which maximizes ductility (95%) but results in steady flow behavior (plastic instability) after initial hardening. The A950 steel has too low stability, causing rapid transformation and early failure.. Limitations: The authors state that the A850 steel, despite its 95% elongation, still exhibits steady flow behavior (plastic instability) which is a drawback for structural applications requiring high strain hardening. Additionally, the A950 steel suffers from seriously reduced elongation due to a transformation rate that is too high.. Future work: The authors propose that the A900 steel, with its outstanding tensile properties and reduced density, gives a promise for automotive applications as highly-deformable high-strength sheets and structural reinforcement components requiring high stiffness.. Quote: "The present work gives a promise for structural applications requiring both reduced specific weight and remarkable deformability."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the fundamental mechanism responsible for the loss of ductility with increasing temperature in single-phase face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys, specifically CrMnFeCoNi?. System: Equiatomic Cr20MnFe20Co20Ni20 (single-phase) and nonequiatomic Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 (dual-phase with Cr-rich σ). Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere, homogenization at 1200°C for 48 hours, hot rolling at 1100°C to 8 mm, cold rolling to 2.4 mm (70% reduction), annealing at 1000°C for 1 hour (single-phase) or 900°C for 1 hour (dual-phase). Test conditions: Quasi-static tensile tests at 25° to 800°C, strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹, samples held at temperature for ~10 min before testing. Findings: Ductility loss in single-phase Cr20MnFe20Co20Ni20 occurs at intermediate temperatures (400° to 700°C) with fracture shortly after ultimate tensile stress.; Fracture mode changes from fully ductile transgranular failure at 25°C to mixed brittle intergranular and ductile transgranular failure at 700°C.; Atom probe tomography reveals nanosized regions (~5 nm thickness) at grain boundaries enriched with Cr, Ni, and Mn after testing at 700°C.; No second-phase precipitates were detected along grain boundaries by XRD, TEM, or SEM-EDS after testing at 700°C.; Cr and Ni segregate separately at grain boundaries, while Ni and Mn tend to cosegregate.; The dual-phase Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 alloy exhibits increased ductility with temperature and no intergranular embrittlement at 600° and 700°C.; Trace elements C and B segregate at grain boundaries but at concentrations (0.2 at% C, 0.008 at% B) insufficient to form carbides or borides.. Mechanism: Ductility loss is caused by the fast segregation of principal elements (Cr, Ni, Mn) into grain boundaries during deformation at intermediate temperatures, forming nanoclusters that reduce grain boundary cohesion and promote crack initiation. The authors propose that Cr and Ni segregate separately due to repulsion, while Ni and Mn cosegregate, potentially forming brittle phases or reducing cohesion via magnetic contributions. Preexisting Cr-rich σ phases can absorb these embrittling elements, preventing their segregation to grain boundaries.. Limitations: The study notes that grain refinement in HEAs can assist the segregation of principal elements to grain boundaries and lead to brittle intermetallic phases, making grain refinement ineffective for avoiding this specific embrittlement. Additionally, the dual-phase alloy designed for proof-of-concept has lower ductility than the single-phase alloy below 500°C.. Future work: The authors suggest that the ductility of HEAs at intermediate temperatures can be further improved if the morphology, dimension, and distribution of secondary phases are optimized further following the proposed GB segregation engineering strategy.. Quote: "Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the physical origins of the exceptional high-temperature strength and strength retention in refractory body-centered-cubic (BCC) high-entropy alloys (HEAs)?. System: NbTaTiV (nominal Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 at.%) and CrMoNbV (nominal CrMoNbV at.%); search space includes the 10-component Al-Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr family.. Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt.% purity elements under argon atmosphere followed by drop-casting into cylindrical rods; NbTaTiV homogenized at 1473 K for 3 days then water-cooled; CrMoNbV tested in the as-cast state.. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression at strain rates of 1 × 10−3 s−1 (NbTaTiV) and 2 × 10−4 s−1 (CrMoNbV); temperatures up to 1173 K; in situ neutron diffraction and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) performed during deformation.. Findings: Neutron diffraction peak broadening analysis yielded q values of -0.6 to -0.4 for NbTaTiV and -2 for CrMoNbV, consistent with edge dislocations and distinct from screw dislocations (+1.9 to +2.1).; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of NbTaTiV deformed at 293 K showed 75% (58 of 77) of dislocations were of edge character.; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of CrMoNbV deformed at 293 K showed 56% (23 of 41) of dislocations were of edge character.; At 1173 K, edge dislocations remained dominant with 82% (27 of 33) in NbTaTiV and 64% (81 of 127) in CrMoNbV.; The CrMoNbV alloy exhibited the highest reported strength at a homologous temperature of 1173 K.; A computationally guided search over 10^7 BCC HEA compositions identified over 10^6 possible ultra-strong high-temperature alloy compositions.; Theoretical predictions for NbTaTiV strength were lower than experimental values by ~300-500 MPa, attributed to 1.6 at.% O+N interstitial impurities.. Mechanism: In complex HEAs, fluctuations in local solute arrangements create large local variations in potential energy, forcing edge dislocations to adopt a low-energy wavy structure; plastic flow requires thermal activation to overcome large energy barriers created by adjacent high-energy environments, enabling high strength retention at elevated temperatures.. Limitations: The theory does not capture the strength plateau observed at 973–1273 K in many BCC HEAs; neutron pattern quality for CrMoNbV was lower than for NbTaTiV, especially at low plastic strains; the theory assumes a homogeneous average alloy which may not fully capture local complexities.. Future work: Propose fabrication and testing of specific alloys (Mo5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo2.5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo6WCrZrHf, Mo2.5TaWV2.5CrZrHf) with predicted strengths of ~2.5-3 GPa at 1300 K; combine design strategy with detailed thermodynamics and high ductility criteria to discover multi-objective alloys.. Quote: "Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations."

card: Paper card. Question: How do specific alloying elements (Nb, Ta, Ti vs. Cr, Mo) influence the deformation mechanisms and creep resistance of Ni-based superalloys at high temperatures?. System: Two single-crystal Ni-based superalloys: ME3 (9.1 wt% η phase formers: Nb, Ta, W, Hf, Ti) and ME501 (13 wt% η phase formers), with ME501 having higher Ta, Hf, and Nb and lower Co and Cr compared to ME3.. Processing: Single crystals were cast, heat-treated to form a bimodal γ-γ′ microstructure, and machined into compression cuboids (1:1:2.5 ratio) via Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM).. Test conditions: Monotonic compression creep tests at 760 °C on [001] oriented samples; ME3 tested at 414 MPa and ME501 at 552 MPa to achieve comparable strain rates of 5 × 10⁻⁹ s⁻¹.. Findings: ME501 exhibited remarkably improved creep resistance compared to ME3 at 760 °C and 552 MPa.; Nanotwinning contributed up to 50% of the plastic strain in ME3 but was not operative in ME501.; In ME501, shear-induced solid-state transformation from γ′ to η phase occurred along stacking faults, whereas ME3 showed segregation of γ-formers (Cr, Mo).; Atomic resolution EDX confirmed Ta and Nb segregate to Wyckoff 2a positions and Al and Ti to Wyckoff 2d positions of the η phase at faults in ME501.; The energy barrier for thickening stacking faults into nanotwins was 364 mJ m⁻² for pure Ni₃Al, 481 mJ m⁻² for ME501 (random solid solution), and 743 mJ m⁻² for the η-phase-segregated fault in ME501.; Energy release upon atomic reordering for twin formation was 375 mJ m⁻² for pure Ni₃Al but only 15 mJ m⁻² for ME3.; Isolated stacking faults in ME501 were identified as superlattice extrinsic stacking faults (SESFs) constrained to the γ′ phase.. Mechanism: The authors propose a 'phase-transformation strengthening' mechanism where high concentrations of η-phase formers (Nb, Ta, Ti) segregate to stacking faults, inducing a shear-induced transformation to a nanoscale η phase. This η phase creates a low-energy structure that significantly increases the energy barrier for the thickening of stacking faults into nanotwins, thereby suppressing the deleterious nanotwinning deformation mode. Conversely, in alloys with γ-formers (Cr, Mo), the fault transforms into a γ-like region that lowers the energy barrier for twin formation.. Limitations: The text notes that the ability to predict mechanical properties for a given alloy remains a major challenge and that the characterization of specific elements in compositionally complex superalloys has historically been qualitative and empirical.. Future work: The authors suggest that this mechanism may be further manipulated through alloying and processing to improve the high-temperature properties of next-generation superalloys for critical structural applications.. Quote: "specific alloying elements inhibit the deleterious deformation mode of nanotwinning at temperatures above 700 °C"

Question: What are the unique elastic and plastic deformation mechanisms of a single-phase BCC NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy at room temperature and elevated temperatures, and how do they compare to conventional BCC alloys?. System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 atomic %). Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, sealed in quartz tubes, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling.. Test conditions: In situ neutron diffraction compression tests at RT, 500°C, 700°C, and 900°C with strain rate of 1 × 10−4 s−1; Resonant Ultrasound Spectroscopy (RUS) from 100 to 650 kHz; First-principles DFT calculations at absolute zero and RT; Machine Learning predictions; HAADF-STEM imaging of 15% deformed samples.. Findings: Yield strength decreased from 1064 MPa at RT to 595 MPa at 900°C.; Work-hardening exponent decreased from 0.2732 at RT to 0.1199 at 900°C.; The alloy exhibits elastically isotropic deformation behavior at RT (Zener anisotropy AZ ≈ 1.2, Universal anisotropy index AU = 0).; Elastic anisotropy gradually increases at elevated temperatures but shows much smaller variation (AZ from 1.2 at RT to 1.6 at 900°C) compared to conventional alloys.; The dominant mobile dislocations during plastic deformation are edge dislocations (<111> {110}), unlike conventional BCC metals where screw dislocations often dominate.; Single-crystal elastic constants calculated via DFT show good agreement with experimental neutron and RUS data, with relative errors of -15.9% (Young's), -16.6% (shear), and -6.0% (bulk) at RT.; The alloy maintains a single BCC solid solution phase with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm up to 900°C.; Pugh ratio (K/G) and Poisson's ratio (ν > 0.26) indicate the material is intrinsically ductile.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the severely distorted lattice in the HEA, caused by the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii, leads to compositional fluctuations that deviate edge dislocation cores from their neutral planes. This creates wavy dislocation lines, which substantially reduces the mobility of edge dislocations, making them the dominant mobile character compared to conventional BCC metals where edge dislocations annihilate easily.. Limitations: The text notes that the validity of theoretical calculation methods for designing elastically isotropic and ductile BCC HEAs was previously lacking experimental validation, though this paper addresses that. It also mentions that the ML model predictions are somewhat unexpected because the Materials Project database contains ordered compounds, not disordered alloys like HEAs, and lattice distortion effects might cause less accurate results.. Future work: The authors state these discoveries may facilitate the development of possible alloy systems for structural material applications and provide a road map toward the discovery and production of newly designed polycrystalline materials.. Quote: "The dominant type of mobile dislocations during plastic deformation could be edge dislocations, which is different from conventional BCC metals."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallics within the fcc phase of a eutectic Al0.7CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy influence its strain-rate dependent mechanical behavior, specifically yield strength, work hardening, and deformation mechanisms under quasi-static versus dynamic loading?. System: Al0.7CoCrFeNi (15 at.% Al, 21.25 at.% each of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni) forming a lamellar dual-phase microstructure of fcc + B2 (with B2 containing bcc nano-precipitates), further modified by L12 precipitation in the fcc phase.. Processing: Melting of elemental constituents, homogenization at 1150 °C for 1 h, cold rolling to 30% reduction, annealing at 1100 °C for 5 mins (CR-H condition), and low-temperature annealing at 580 °C for 24 h (CR-H-580 condition).. Test conditions: Quasi-static tensile loading at a strain rate of 10−3 s−1 and dynamic compressive loading using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) at a strain rate of 2 × 103 s−1.. Findings: The CR-H-580 condition with L12 precipitates exhibited a yield strength of ~1080 MPa and UTS of ~1370 MPa under quasi-static loading, compared to ~770 MPa YS and ~1090 MPa UTS for the CR-H condition.; Under dynamic loading (2 × 103 s−1), flow stresses reached ~1800 MPa for the CR-H-580 condition without failure up to 20% strain.; The introduction of L12 precipitates resulted in a precipitation strengthening of ~310 MPa, which compares reasonably well with the Orowan model prediction of ~360 MPa.; The steady-state work hardening rate increased from ~3000 MPa in the CR-H condition to >4000 MPa in the CR-H-580 condition.; The strain rate sensitivity (SRS) parameter (m) at 1% flow stress was 0.018 for CR-H and 0.017 for CR-H-580, indicating L12 precipitation did not significantly alter SRS.; Post-deformation analysis revealed that the L12 phase disorders under both quasi-static and dynamic deformation, forming anti-phase boundaries.; High density of twins (approx. 20 nm thick) was observed in the fcc phase under dynamic testing, whereas only fine-scale nano-twins were seen under quasi-static testing.; APT analysis showed L12 precipitates have a radius of ~3–5 nm, a volume fraction of ~9.5% within the fcc lamellae, and a composition of ~56.4 at.% Ni and ~35.8 at.% Al.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strength increase to the Orowan dislocation bowing and bypass mechanism by coherent L12 precipitates. The high work hardening is explained by the capability of the lamellar structure to store high dislocation densities at interfaces and the formation of anti-phase boundaries upon L12 disordering. The lack of significant change in SRS is rationalized by the presence of precipitate-free channels near the lamellar boundaries which act as sites for high dislocation storage, and the thermally activated nature of the coherent L12 precipitates.. Limitations: The text notes that detailed first-principles computational studies are needed to establish the exact site-occupancies of elements within the ordered L12 structure due to the unusually high Al content. It also mentions that the B2 lamellae are not continuous but pinched off at the microscopic scale.. Future work: The authors state that detailed first-principles, electronic structure based computational studies need to be coupled with experimental observations to establish the site-occupancies of different elements within the ordered L12 structure.. Quote: "Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength."

card: Paper card. Question: How to achieve a simultaneous balance of high fracture strength and high ductility in high-entropy alloys while overcoming inferior castability and compositional segregation?. System: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); bulk ingot weight ~2.5 kg.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; elevated temperature tests at 600°C and 700°C at strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1; cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction followed by tensile testing at 2 × 10−3 s−1.. Findings: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.; Room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%.; The proof stress was 75 MPa, while the fracture stress reached close to 1.2 GPa (true stress condition).; At 600°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 806 MPa and elongation of 33.7%.; At 700°C, the alloy maintained a fracture stress of 538 MPa and elongation of 22.9%.; Cold rolling with 8% reduction increased the true fracture stress to 1265 MPa while maintaining 9.9% elongation.; The density of the EHEA was measured to be 7.38 g/cm3.; The ratio of fracture strength to proof stress (σUTS/σ0.2) was close to 16.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the unprecedented strain hardening and balanced properties to the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. When dislocations pass through soft fcc phases, the hard B2 phases, including nanoscale precipitates, pin the movement of dislocations resulting in significant work hardening.. Limitations: The text notes that the mechanism for the low elastic limit (proof stress) is still unclear at this stage.. Future work: Further exploration of new EHEAs will be based on physical metallurgy principles using atomic radius, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration; thermodynamics calculations based on the CALPHAD method can provide guidance once reliable databases are established; the potential for producing ultrahigh strength components after large plastic deformation awaits further investigations.. Quote: "To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single consolidated target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear resistance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min; annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter) with max force 3 mN; tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C using 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation yielded an average hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa.; Nanopillar compression tests revealed a high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa (yield strength 10.7 ± 0.8 GPa).; Annealing at 300 °C reduced surface roughness to 2 nm (Sa) and significantly improved film adhesion compared to the as-deposited state.; The annealed film showed an average coefficient of friction (COF) of 0.25 at RT and 1.5 at 300 °C.; Wear rates were 6.4 × 10⁻⁶ mm³/N m at RT and 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/N m at 300 °C, which are 10² times lower than 304 stainless steel at RT.; The film hardness was ~20% higher than previously reported RHEA films in the literature.. Mechanism: The high hardness and strength are attributed to nanocrystalline grain size, grain boundary strengthening, solid solution hardening, lattice distortion, and sluggish diffusion. The strengthening mechanism in nanopillars shifts from dislocation-controlled to grain-boundary-controlled plastic deformation, leading to intergranular fracture. Annealing improves adhesion and stability, while the formation of CuO at 300 °C influences tribological behavior.. Limitations: The as-deposited film showed excessive plastic deformation, smearing, and radial cracks due to low adhesion, leading to a sharp increase in COF after 15 m of sliding. The film composition showed in-depth nonhomogeneity, being rich in W, Ta, and Mo at the surface and V at the interface. The high COF at 300 °C was attributed to tribochemical reactions and oxide formation on the counterball.. card: Paper card. Question: How can the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a continuous ordered B2 matrix be improved while maintaining high yield strength?. System: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr (Refractory High Entropy Alloy). Processing: 1. Vacuum/argon arc melting followed by hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C for 2 hours under 210 MPa argon. 2. Homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 hours followed by slow cooling (10 °C/min) to room temperature (Condition 1). 3. Solutionizing Condition 1 at 1400 °C for 20 min followed by water quenching (Condition 2). 4. Annealing Condition 2 at 600 °C for 120 hrs followed by water quenching (Condition 3).. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) and 600 °C uniaxial compression testing at a strain rate of 0.001 s−1; Vickers microhardness (4.9 N load, 15 s dwell); Microstructural characterization via SEM, TEM, and Atom Probe Tomography (APT).. Findings: Condition (1) (continuous B2 matrix) exhibited a yield strength of 2035 MPa but only 4.5% compressive strain before fracture.; Condition (2) (single-phase weakly ordered BCC) showed high ductility with no fracture after 60% true strain but lower yield strength (1065 MPa).; Condition (3) (inverted microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates in continuous BCC matrix) achieved a yield strength of 1345 MPa and 16.9% peak strain with fracture at 38% strain.; At 600 °C, Condition (3) showed anomalous strengthening with a yield strength of 1423 MPa (higher than its RT value of 1345 MPa) and 16.2% plasticity.; APT analysis revealed strong elemental partitioning: B2 phase is rich in Al and Zr, while BCC phase is rich in Nb and Ta.; The microstructure of Condition (3) consists of discrete B2 precipitates (~50 nm) within a continuous disordered BCC matrix, contrasting with Condition (1) where B2 is the continuous matrix.; Condition (1) hardness was 562 ± 16 HV, Condition (2) was 405 ± 11 HV, and Condition (3) was 475 ± 12 HV.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the poor ductility in Condition (1) is caused by the continuous ordered B2 matrix, which is inherently brittle. The improved ductility in Condition (3) is attributed to the 'inversion' of the microstructure, where the continuous phase becomes the more ductile disordered BCC matrix, while the hard B2 phase exists as discrete precipitates providing strengthening. The anomalous strengthening at 600 °C in Condition (3) is speculated to result from competing slip systems in the complex B2 phase (e.g., <001>{110} and <111>{112}) leading to sessile kinks or dislocation debris, similar to mechanisms in Ni3Al.. Limitations: The authors state that the details of the strengthening mechanisms are beyond the scope of the study and that the explanation for the anomalous strengthening at 600 °C is highly speculative. They note that applying classical precipitation hardening models requires parameters (lattice misfit, elastic properties, fault energies) that are difficult to quantify in this complex RHEA.. Future work: The authors recommend additional scientific studies to establish the influence of concentrated alloy additions on precipitation strengthening parameters, further investigation of deformation mechanisms at room temperature and 600 °C, and additional studies at higher temperatures and under tensile loading.. card: Paper card. Question: How does substrate deposition temperature influence the phase evolution, microstructure, and mechanical properties of HfNbTiVZr high-entropy thin films compared to bulk alloys?. System: HfNbTiVZr near-equimolar thin films (XPS determined composition: Hf21Nb20Ti20V18Zr21). Processing: Non-reactive DC-magnetron sputtering in ultra-high vacuum (<5 × 10−8 Pa) using elemental targets; substrates (Si(001) or Al2O3(00l)) biased to −50 V and heated to three temperatures: room temperature (RT), 275 °C, and 450 °C.. Test conditions: Mechanical properties measured via nanoindentation (Berkovich tip); structural analysis via XRD, pole figures, and TEM/SAED; chemical analysis via XPS and EDS.. Findings: Films deposited at room temperature exhibit an amorphous microstructure with a hardness of 6.5 ± 0.3 GPa.; Films deposited at 275 °C crystallize into a single-phase body-centred cubic (bcc) solid solution with a hardness of 7.9 ± 0.3 GPa.; Films deposited at 450 °C on Si substrates form a dual-phase structure of bcc matrix and C15 Laves phase precipitates, reaching a peak hardness of 9.2 ± 0.4 GPa.; Films deposited at 450 °C on sapphire substrates form a dual-phase structure of bcc matrix and C14 Laves phase precipitates.; The lattice parameter of the bcc phase decreases from 3.42 Å (at 275 °C) to 3.39 Å (at 450 °C).; All thin films exhibit significantly higher hardness than reported literature values for bulk HfNbTiVZr alloys (3.8 GPa).; Films deposited at 275 °C show a strong <110> preferred orientation, while films at 450 °C on Si show a shift to <100> orientation.. Mechanism: The high quenching rates (>10^6 K/s) during magnetron sputtering combined with low ad-atom mobility at low temperatures enable the synthesis of amorphous phases not accessible in bulk. At higher temperatures, surface diffusion is much faster than bulk diffusion, allowing segregation and Laves phase formation at lower temperatures (450 °C) than in bulk annealing (>600 °C). The specific Laves phase (C14 vs C15) depends on the substrate, likely due to differences in diffusivities and Nb availability during growth.. Limitations: Peak overlaps in the θ–2θ diffractograms for films on sapphire at 450 °C did not allow unambiguous separation between the hcp phase and the C14 Laves phase, though the latter was favored based on lattice parameter stability and pole figure fits.. Future work: Further studies are required to determine why the substrate affects the C14/C15 formation and to understand the role of Nb diffusivity and availability during film growth compared to solid-state transformation.. Quote: "Films deposited at room temperature exhibit an amorphous microstructure and are 6.5 GPa hard."

Question: What are the temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation mechanisms of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM), and how do they correlate with the unique microstructure formed during the process?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using pre-alloyed spherical powder (average diameter 27.2 µm); Laser power 90 W, scan speed 600 mm/s, hatch space 80 µm, layer thickness 25 µm, volumetric energy density 75 J/mm³, 180° rotation scanning pattern, high-purity Ar atmosphere.. Test conditions: Compression tests performed at 25, 500, 600, 700, 800, and 900 °C; initial strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; engineering strain limit 0.4; specimens preheated at 10 °C/min; MoS₂ spray used as lubricant.. Findings: SLM-built HEA exhibited a yield strength of 778.4 MPa at room temperature, significantly higher than annealed (254.2 MPa) and other AM-processed (approx. 519 MPa) variants.; The average dislocation density was measured at 1.88 × 10¹⁴ m⁻², which is higher than in homogenized HEA.; Nano-sized Mn₂O₃ precipitates with an average size of 27.3 nm were identified at cell structure boundaries.; Average grain sizes varied by direction: 5.98 µm (Building Direction), 12.93 µm (Transverse Direction), and 15.66 µm (Scanning Direction).; Type-C serration occurred at 600 °C with a stress drop amplitude (∆σ) of approximately 4.5 MPa.; Activation energy for deformation at 600 °C was measured at 335 kJ/mol, indicating cooperative lattice diffusion rather than interstitial solute diffusion.; Work hardening occurred from room temperature to 600 °C, while work softening occurred at temperatures higher than 700 °C due to dynamic recrystallization.; Ultra-fine recrystallized grains with an average size of 378 nm were observed at grain boundaries after deformation at 700 °C.. Mechanism: Superior mechanical properties at low temperatures (25–600 °C) are attributed to fine grain size, high dislocation density, and nano-sized Mn₂O₃ precipitates providing dislocation forest hardening and Orowan strengthening. At high temperatures (≥700 °C), dislocation forest hardening and Orowan strengthening remain dominant as matrix and grain boundary strengthening diminish. Deformation mechanisms shift from slip and deformation twinning (25–600 °C) to slip and partial dynamic recrystallization (≥700 °C). The delay in full recrystallization and strain softening up to 900 °C is caused by the Zener drag effect from Mn₂O₃ precipitates and retarding pressure from migrated grain boundaries.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that previous studies on AM-processed HEA were limited to fundamental investigations and room temperature properties.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work, but implies the need to further understand the correlations among microstructure, properties, and deformation mechanisms to tune alloys for high-performance applications.. Quote: "SLM-built HEA has a higher dislocation density of 1.88 × 1014 m−2 as compared to the homogenized HEA."

card: Paper card. Question: Is polymorphism still possible in entropy-stabilized high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that are generally believed to possess extremely high structural stability and maintain a single-phase structure?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (Cantor's alloy). Processing: Synthesized via gas-atomization (melt injected into high purity Ar at 4 MPa pressure); subjected to hydrostatic compression up to ~41 GPa using a diamond anvil cell (DAC) with helium as pressure-transmitting medium; subsequently heated using resistive heating (up to 723 K) or double-sided Nd:YLF laser heating (up to ~1,400 K) at various pressures (6, 14, 26 GPa).. Test conditions: Room temperature compression up to ~41 GPa; heating at ambient pressure up to 723 K; heating at 6, 14, and 26 GPa up to ~1,400 K; in situ synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring.. Findings: The fcc-to-hcp polymorphic transition starts at approximately 22 GPa and almost completes at approximately 41 GPa.; The phase transition is irreversible; the hcp phase is retained when pressure is released to ambient conditions.; The hcp phase remains stable up to 633 K at ambient pressure before transforming back to fcc.; At 26 GPa, the critical temperature for the hcp-to-fcc transition is approximately 1,400 K.; The isothermal bulk modulus (B0) is 153.9±3.0 GPa for the fcc phase and 150.2±4.6 GPa for the hcp phase.; The c/a ratio of the hcp phase remained almost constant at 1.62±0.01 during compression and decompression.; The transition is sluggish, with fcc and hcp phases coexisting over a wide pressure range of ~22 to ~41 GPa.; Decompression from different maximum pressures yields fcc/hcp composites with tunable fractions.. Mechanism: The transition occurs because the hcp structure is thermodynamically more favorable at lower temperatures and high pressures, while the fcc phase is stable at higher temperatures and lower pressures; the transition is kinetically hindered by high energy barriers and low stacking fault energy (~20 mJ m−2), requiring high pressure to overcome these barriers to form the hcp phase.. Limitations: The transition is sluggish and irreversible, making it difficult to determine the real equilibrium phase boundary (Clapeyron coexistence curve) experimentally; grain size was not small enough for statistically reliable Rietveld refinement of volume fractions; overshooting often exists due to high energy barriers.. Future work: The authors suggest that this behavior could be general in various HEAs and propose new avenues for tailoring HEA properties via polymorphic transition-induced HEA composites, particularly at cryogenic temperatures where transition pressure could be largely decreased.. Quote: "The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: Does hydrogen exposure cause catastrophic failure (hydrogen embrittlement) or can it improve mechanical properties in an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (Cantor's alloy). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of pure elements (Co20Cr20Fe20Mn20Ni20 at.%), hot-rolling at 900 °C (50% reduction), homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h, water-quenching, cold-rolling (60% reduction), and annealing at 900 °C for 3 min followed by water-quenching.. Test conditions: Electrochemical hydrogen charging in 0.1 M NaOH + 0.05 g·L−1 CH4N2S at pH = 13 and 25 °C; pre-charging durations of 12 h (15 mA·cm−2), 72 h (25 mA·cm−2), and 240 h (100 mA·cm−2); in-situ tensile testing at a rate of 1 × 10−4 S−1 with continuous charging.. Findings: The hydrogen-free alloy exhibited an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 545 MPa and total elongation of ~68%.; Pre-charging for 12 h at 15 mA·cm−2 (8.01 wt.ppm H) increased UTS to 571 MPa and uniform elongation to ~71%.; Pre-charging for 72 h at 25 mA·cm−2 (15.22 wt.ppm H) increased UTS to 588 MPa and uniform elongation to ~71%, representing ~7.9% and ~4.4% increases over the hydrogen-free sample.; Pre-charging for 240 h at 100 mA·cm−2 (33.25 wt.ppm H) showed a slightly reduced increment in strength and ductility compared to the 15.22 wt.ppm sample, suggesting saturation.; Hydrogen alloying did not exert significant effects on the yield strength of the alloy.; The hydrogen alloyed HEA with 15.22 wt.ppm H exhibited the highest strain-hardening rate among all conditions.; The density of deformation nanotwins significantly increased in hydrogen alloyed samples compared to the hydrogen-free alloy.; The intrinsic stacking fault energy of the alloy is ~19 mJ·m2, which is reduced further by hydrogen.. Mechanism: Hydrogen reduces the stacking fault energy and phase stability of the f.c.c. lattice, which triggers more intense nanotwinning upon loading. This increased nanotwin density enhances the work-hardening rate via the 'dynamic Hall-Petch' effect (continuous grain fragmentation and reduced dislocation mean free path), thereby simultaneously increasing strength and ductility. At very high hydrogen concentrations, unfavorable mechanisms like hydrogen enhanced localized plasticity or surface cracking compete with the beneficial twinning, leading to saturation or slight reduction in gains.. Limitations: The text notes that at the highest hydrogen concentration (33.25 wt.ppm), the increment in strength and ductility was reduced, likely due to a competition between beneficial nanotwining and unfavorable mechanisms like hydrogen enhanced localized plasticity or initial surface cracks caused by high surface hydrogen concentration.. Future work: The authors propose that these results open new pathways for the design of strong, ductile, and hydrogen tolerant materials by utilizing hydrogen to tune beneficial hardening mechanisms rather than viewing it solely as a harmful impurity.. Quote: "hydrogen in an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) leads not to catastrophic weakening, but instead increases both, its strength and ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the specific role of each cation in the high-entropy oxide Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2O during electrochemical cycling, and how does their synergy explain the 'cocktail effect' and structural reversibility in conversion-type reactions?. System: Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2O (High Entropy Oxide). Processing: Nebulized spray pyrolysis (NSP) at 1150 °C using a mist speed of 40 mL/h and N2 carrier gas; electrode preparation involved mixing with Super C65 and PVDF (7:2:1 ratio) on copper foil, dried at 80 °C.. Test conditions: Coin-type half-cells with Li foil counter/reference, 1 M LiPF6 in EC/EMC electrolyte, cycled between 0.01 V and 3.0 V at 50 mA/g; characterized via XAS, S/TEM, 4D-STEM, electron tomography, and in-situ TEM-STM conductivity measurements.. Findings: Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn are reduced to metallic states during the first discharge, forming a CoNiCu alloy and LiZn phase.; Upon charging, Ni and Cu remain metallic, while Zn is almost fully reoxidized to the 2+ state and a large fraction of Co reoxidizes.; The discharged sample consists of a metallic phase (Co, Ni, Cu) and an oxide phase (O, Mg, Li) with Zn forming a separate LiZn nanophase.; The metallic phase forms a 3D dendritic network at grain boundaries and inside grains, providing a continuous electron transport path.; The oxide phase (Mg-dominated) is semi-coherent with the metallic phase and accommodates Li+ ions.; The charged particle exhibits significantly higher electrical conductivity (0.1 µA at 15 V) compared to the insulating as-prepared sample.; The structural features (phase separation and network) are maintained after 5 cycles, confirming high reversibility.; The theoretical capacity for the first discharge is 687 mAh/g (611 mAh/g from CoNiCu + 76 mAh/g from LiZn).. Mechanism: The synergy arises from distinct cation roles: (i) Zn and Co provide electrochemical capacity; (ii) Mg2+ is electrochemically inert and stabilizes the oxide nanophase that accommodates Li+; (iii) Cu and Ni remain metallic to form a 3D conductive backbone. This self-assembled nanostructure bypasses the need for pre-nanostructuring, mechanically stabilizes the particle, and ensures fast reaction kinetics by reducing the reaction path to the nanometer level.. Limitations: The initial HEO structure cannot be restored during the first charge cycle because the high configurational entropy required for the single-phase solid solution is only effective at the synthesis temperature (>877 °C) and is insufficient to stabilize the structure at room temperature during conversion reactions. Additionally, the exact presence of nano/sub-nanometer scale Li2O aggregates cannot be ruled out due to detection limits.. Future work: The findings can help to design new conversion-type materials for the application as battery electrodes by utilizing elemental diversity to optimize multi-cation electrode materials.. Quote: "The more electronegative elements form an electrochemically inert 3-dimensional metallic nano-network enabling electron transport."

card: Paper card. Question: How does entropy stabilization in transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) influence reversible lithium storage capacity, cycling stability, and the underlying reaction mechanism compared to medium entropy oxides?. System: Transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) with composition (Co0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Ni0.2Zn0.2)O; compared to 4-cation medium entropy oxides (MEO) such as (Co0.25Cu0.25Zn0.25Ni0.25)O and (Co0.25Cu0.25Mg0.25Zn0.25)O. Processing: Nebulized Spray Pyrolysis (NSP) at 1150 °C; 4-cation systems required post-annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h under ambient atmosphere; electrodes cast with 63 wt% active material, 22 wt% Super C65, 15 wt% PVA binder. Test conditions: Galvanostatic cycling in Li-metal coin cells, voltage range 0.01–3 V vs. Li+/Li, specific currents from 50 to 3000 mA g−1, room temperature, 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DMC or EC/EMC electrolyte. Findings: The 5-cation TM-HEO cycled over 300 cycles at 200 mA g−1 with specific capacities stabilizing around 650 mAh g−1 after initial activation.; The 5-cation system achieved a specific capacity of 770 mAh g−1 after 100 cycles following a rate increase to 3 A g−1 for 5 cycles.; Medium entropy oxides (4-cation systems) showed rapid capacity degradation, with the Co-removed variant failing completely after ~10 cycles.; The Coulombic efficiency of the 5-cation TM-HEO stabilized between 99.4% and 99.95% in the range of cycles 60–400.; The 4-cation system without Zn (TM-MEO(-Zn)) exhibited a two-step oxidation process at 1.7 V and 2.2 V, unlike the single-step oxidation of the 5-cation system.; High-loading electrodes (2.3 mg cm−2) maintained Coulombic efficiencies >98.5% and an areal capacity of 1.3 mAh cm−2 after 30 cycles.; No metallic phases or Cu dendrites were detected via TEM/EDX after 100 cycles, despite the conversion reaction mechanism.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the rock-salt structure is preserved as a permanent host matrix during the entire conversion process. While some cations (e.g., Co, Cu) are reduced to metallic states during lithiation, they remain 'trapped' within the defect-rich rock-salt lattice stabilized by unreduced cations (e.g., Mg, Ni). This entropy stabilization lowers the Gibbs free energy, favoring the re-incorporation of reduced cations into the original lattice sites upon delithiation, preventing phase separation and structural collapse.. Limitations: The theoretical capacity cannot be predicted with high accuracy due to unknown additional processes like Zn-Li alloying or intermetallic formation; some 4-cation systems (TM-MEO(-Mg) and TM-MEO(-Ni)) could not be synthesized as single-phase compounds even at high temperatures.. Future work: Further investigations should be pursued to explore the full potential of high entropy oxide electrode materials, including the addition of other cations (Fe, Mn, Cr, V) to develop a modular method for tailoring electrodes to specific needs.. Quote: "The stabilization effect of entropy brings significant benefits for the storage capacity retention of high entropy oxides and greatly improves the cycling stability."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the specific lithiation and delithiation mechanism of Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2O (TM-HEO) anodes, particularly regarding the reversibility of the conversion reaction and the origin of the observed high capacity?. System: Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2O (TM-HEO) and comparative systems (CoCuMgNi)O and (CoCuNiZn)O. Processing: Solid-state reaction of commercial metal oxides (MgO, ZnO, CuO, NiO, CoO) at 1000 °C for 6 h with a ramp of 10 °C min–1; anode slurry prepared with 70 wt% active material, 20% carbon black, 10% PVDF binder, cast on copper or carbon cloth, dried at 80 °C under vacuum. Test conditions: Swagelok-type three-electrode cells with metallic Li reference/counter, 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DMC (50:50 vol%) electrolyte, cycled galvanostatically between 3.00 and 0.01 V vs Li+/Li at 0.1 C; operando XAS performed at Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn K-edges during GITT steps. Findings: The first lithiation capacity is 1325 mAh g–1 and the first delithiation capacity is 700 mAh g–1, resulting in a Coulombic efficiency of about 53%.; Cu is the first element reduced, starting at Q = 45 mAh g–1 (1.2–0.9 V), converting sequentially from Cu(II) to Cu(I) and then to metallic Cu(0).; Metallic Co appears at Q = 135 mAh g–1 (0.8 V) and metallic Ni at Q = 180 mAh g–1 (0.7 V).; The HEO rock-salt structure remains intact for approximately 60% of the lithiation capacity before collapsing at Q > 400 mAh g–1.; At the end of the first lithiation cycle, the oxide molar fractions are 0.4(1) for Co and 0.3(1) for Ni, indicating incomplete conversion.; The conversion reaction is irreversible; metals and oxides remain segregated and electrochemically inert during subsequent cycling.; Removing Zn or Mg results in significantly lower capacity: (CoCuMgNi)O stabilizes at ~190 mAh g–1, while (CoCuNiZn)O capacity drops close to zero.; The reversible capacity observed in the full TM-HEO system is attributed to alloying/dealloying mechanisms involving Li with Zn and Mg.. Mechanism: The authors propose a two-stage mechanism: (i) a sequential, irreversible conversion reaction where Cu, Co, and Ni reduce to metals and Li2O, causing the HEO structure to collapse after ~60% capacity due to demixing and loss of long-range order; (ii) a reversible alloying/dealloying mechanism involving Li with the remaining Mg and Zn (and potentially nanosized segregated metals acting as catalysts), which accounts for the high specific capacity and cycling reversibility despite the irreversible conversion of the transition metals.. Limitations: The study notes that the conversion reaction is incomplete and irreversible, leading to the final collapse of the HEO rock-salt structure and the formation of electrochemically inert segregated metals and oxides. Additionally, the large particle size (microsized) and the complexity of the reaction mechanism make the exact contribution of pseudocapacitive effects difficult to isolate, though the authors argue it is not the primary source of capacity.. Future work: The authors suggest that understanding the formation mechanism during lithiation/delithiation is fundamental to optimize the system, and they imply that further studies on the state of charge heterogeneity and the role of nanosized full-field X-ray spectro-microscopy are needed to address the critical challenge of compositional inhomogeneity.. Quote: "The conversion is irreversible and incomplete, leading to the final collapse of the HEO rock-salt structure."

Paper card. Question: What is the specific lithiation/delithiation mechanism in high-entropy oxides (HEOs) with rock-salt structure, and how does configurational entropy influence the reversibility and final phase state?. System: Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2O (TM-HEO) and related compositions (CoCuMgNi)O, (CoCuNiZn)O. Processing: Operando and ex situ XAS measurements combined with electrochemical and microstructural characterization; galvanostatic cycling at 0.1 C. Test conditions: Li-ion cells and Na cells; current density of 0.1 C; voltage range including 0.8 V and >1.0 V. Findings: The first lithiation cycle peak for CuO reduction ranges from 1.0 to 1.5 V depending on the presence or absence of ZnO and MgO.; Sodiation/desodiation processes show serious inefficiency with specific capacity significantly lower than 80 mAh g–1 at 0.1 C.; The lithiation process is incomplete and irreversible, leading to a mixture of M and MO with a variable molar ratio.; A significant fraction of Zn is found in the metallic state at the end of the charging process, proving ZnO participates in the conversion mechanism.; Despite rock-salt structure collapse, the cell delivers a specific capacity higher than 600 mAh g–1 at 0.1 C with Coulombic efficiency very close to 1.; The rock-salt structure maintains up to 60% of charge before the first traces of metallic Co appear around 0.8 V.; EDX maps show the metal distribution is highly nonhomogeneous at the end of lithiation.. Mechanism: The redox reaction occurs via a multistep process dependent on the TMs' reduction potential. The process is irreversible with large entropy production (ΔSi > 0), forcing the system to display no crystalline order at the end to satisfy thermodynamic requirements, as a crystalline alloy would not increase entropy. The high capacity is ascribed to alloying/dealloying reactions typical of anodes like ZnO and MgO.. Limitations: The rock-salt structure is intended to collapse, and the specific composition Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2O is not suitable for use as an anode in LIBs despite promising performances.. Future work: Further strategies of phase stabilization should be investigated by modulating the type of metal, number of cations, stoichiometry, and morphology, and by exploring other structures such as spinel.. Quote: "The only way that is left to the system to increase the entropy as required by the irreversibility condition (ΔSi > 0) is to display no crystalline order at the end of the process."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the deformation mechanisms and strain-hardening behaviors of 〈001〉-oriented fcc dual-phase FeCoCrNiAl0.5 at room and cryogenic temperatures?. System: FeCoCrNiAl0.5 (dual-phase fcc dendrites with bcc/B2 interdendritic network and precipitates). Processing: Bridgman technique ingot preparation in Ar atmosphere, homogenization at 1373K for 24 h, annealing at 1123K for 1 h, water quench, electro-discharge machining (EDM) to 4 mm × 4 mm × 8 mm, grinding to 4000 grit, vibration-polishing for EBSD. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression at 77K (liquid nitrogen) and 293K (room temperature) up to ~35% total axial strain; ex-situ digital image correlation (DIC) with 0.08 μm/pixel resolution; EBSD and TEM analysis. Findings: Hardening rate saturates at ~6 GPa above 23% total axial strain at both 77K and 293K.; Stress levels exceed 1800 MPa at ~35% total axial strain without failure at either temperature.; The fcc component carries the larger part of the plastic strain (mean strain ~3% in fcc vs ~1% in bcc/B2 at ~2% total strain).; Deformation twinning is observed in the fcc phase at both 77K and 293K, but only above 23% axial strain.; Slip activity is found exclusively in the bcc/B2 phase, with no deformation twinning observed there.; Increasing temperature from 77K to 293K raises stress levels by 250–350 MPa but leaves the hardening rate variation unaffected.; The hardening rate increase of >2 GPa beyond 23% strain is present even at room temperature.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the substantial hardening to the combined action of fcc–bcc/B2 interphase boundaries acting as obstacles, extensive deformation twinning in the fcc phase which strongly hardens secondary systems, and fine dense bcc/B2 precipitates inside the fcc dendrites. They specifically note that twin-related interactions are far more important for strengthening than pure slip interactions, and that dislocation reactions at fcc-bcc/B2 interfaces and fcc twin boundaries create residual barriers.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the intricate microstructure and chemical gradients add intricacy to the stress-strain response and that further work is needed to unravel the influence of the minor phase volume fraction and distribution.. Future work: The authors propose that future work should focus on in-situ DIC, nanomechanical testing, and varying heterointerface amounts to differentiate contributions. They also suggest work on the effects of composition on intrinsic energy barriers and composition optimization to develop novel HEAs with higher work-hardening.. Quote: "As a result, the hardening rate associated saturates at the unusual high value of ~6 GPa."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high pressure induce a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase in the prototypical face-centered cubic (fcc) high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi, and what are the mechanisms and retention characteristics of this transformation?. System: CrMnFeCoNi (near-equiatomic solid solution of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni). Processing: Arc-melting of equimolar constituent metals under Ar, drop casting, annealing at 1,200 °C for 24 h, powdering, and loading into a diamond anvil cell with silicone oil pressure medium and Au pressure standard; pressure increased stepwise to 54.1 GPa and decreased at ~1 GPa min⁻¹. Test conditions: Ambient temperature, pressures up to 54.1 GPa, angle-dispersive X-ray diffraction (λ=0.4959 Å). Findings: The fcc-to-hcp transformation begins at approximately 14 GPa.; The transformation is sluggish, occurring over a pressure range of >40 GPa.; The volume collapse accompanying the transformation is 0.6(4)%.; The bulk modulus of the initial fcc phase is 150(3) GPa.; The bulk modulus of the high-pressure hcp phase is 141(8) GPa.; Upon decompression from 54.1 GPa, 56(2)% of the material remains in the hcp phase at ambient pressure.; Upon decompression from 26.8 GPa, 34(1)% of the material remains in the hcp phase at ambient pressure.; Roughly 60% of the hcp volume is retained after depressurization regardless of the maximum pressure achieved.. Mechanism: The transformation is driven by the pressure-induced suppression of local magnetic moments (primarily Fe), which destabilizes the fcc structure; the sluggish kinetics are attributed to the proportionality between pressure and the energy barrier for stacking fault formation.. Limitations: The text notes that the hcp phase is retained due to kinetic hindrance (trapping of atoms and lattice strain) rather than thermodynamic stability, and that rapid pressure quenching might be needed to enhance retention.. Future work: The authors suggest that removing Fe from the alloy might enhance hcp stability and reduce the critical pressure for formation, and that high-pressure processing could be used to tailor mixtures of hard hcp and ductile fcc phases.. Quote: "This martensitic transformation begins at 14 GPa and is attributed to suppression of the local magnetic moments, destabilizing the initial fcc structure."

card: Paper card. Question: How do new Ti-rich BCC high-entropy alloys designed using the Bo-Md approach deform, and do they exhibit transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) to achieve high strength and ductility?. System: Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5, Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2, and Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta7Sn5 (in at%). Processing: Vacuum arc melting to fabricate ingots; tensile specimens (4 mm length × 1 mm width × 0.8 mm thickness) cut from as-cast alloys; tensile tests at room temperature with a constant strain-rate of 10−3 s−1 until fracture. Test conditions: Room temperature; constant strain-rate of 10−3 s−1; microstructural analysis via EBSD and TEM on fractured specimens. Findings: The alloy Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 showed the highest yield strength of 407 MPa and tensile strength of 925 MPa.; The alloy Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 showed a yield strength of 121 MPa and a tensile strength of 574 MPa.; The ratio of maximum tensile strength to yield strength was 2.2 for Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 and 4.7 for Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5.; All alloys maintained high ductility with engineering plastic strain greater than 10%.; Microstructural observations confirmed the transformation of the BCC (β) matrix to HCP (α′) martensite during deformation.; The transformed α′ fraction was maximum in the Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 alloy, which exhibited the highest tensile strength and ductility.; Crystallographic analysis indicated a strong variant selection with (1 1 0)β//(0 0 0 1)α′ and [1 − 1 1]β//[1 1 − 2 0]α′.; Deformation twins were observed inside the transformed α′ phase in the Ti38Zr25Hf25Ta10Sn2 alloy.. Mechanism: The authors explain the high strain-hardening and ductility through the TRIP effect, where the metastable soft β phase transforms into a relatively hard α′ phase. This transformation generates distinct phase boundaries that dynamically refine the effective grain size (dynamic Hall–Petch effect), decrease the mean free path for dislocation slip, and induce geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) to create long-range stress fields. Additionally, the transformed α′ phase deforms by twinning or dislocation slip, and the specific Burgers orientation relationship ensures a low-energy interface that facilitates the transformation.. Limitations: The text notes that the yield strength of the Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 alloy in this study (121 MPa) was significantly lower than a previously reported value (540 MPa) due to the coarse initial grain size (d ~ 220 µm) compared to the previous study (d ~ 40 µm).. Future work: Controlling the microstructure, especially decreasing the initial grain size using appropriate thermo-mechanical processing route, might result in a remarkable increment of strength and ductility; further optimization of microstructural parameters is being done and will be reported in a future article.. Quote: "The alloys showed exceptionally high strain-hardening and ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the metastability of the γ matrix in a dual-phase high entropy alloy be tuned via alloy chemistry and processing to achieve extremely high strength and sustained work hardening ability?. System: Fe42Mn28Co10Cr15Si5 (at.%) dual-phase high entropy alloy (DP-5Si-HEA). Processing: Vacuum arc-casting followed by multi-pass friction stir processing (M-pass) with 3 overlapping passes; rotational rates decremented from 650 RPM (pass 1) to 350 RPM (pass 2) to 250 RPM (pass 3) with Argon shrouding. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at an initial strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The M-pass specimen exhibited a yield strength (YS) of 950 MPa and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 1.15 GPa.; Grain refinement via M-pass reduced grain size from 100 µm (as-cast) to 1.3 µm.; The as-cast material showed a YS of 400 MPa and ductility of 7%, while the M-pass specimen achieved 12% total elongation.; The work hardening rate (θ) for the M-pass specimen reached 3612 MPa at the onset of the transformation-dominated sub-stage.; In the as-cast condition, the γ phase fraction decreased from 94% to 11% after complete tensile deformation.; In the M-pass condition, the γ phase fraction decreased by approximately 90% after complete tensile deformation.; The M-pass specimen contained 88% γ phase and 12% ε phase prior to deformation, whereas the as-cast condition had a different phase distribution.. Mechanism: The addition of Si decreases the stacking fault energy and increases the metastability of the γ matrix, promoting rapid γ → ε transformation (TRIP) and deformation twinning in the ε phase. The fine grain size (1.3 µm) provides high grain boundary area that exerts back stress, ensuring uniform strain partitioning between the γ and ε phases, which sustains the work hardening rate and prevents premature failure.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The authors propose that tuning the metastability of the γ phase by adding non-transition elements like Si is a new pathway for designing HEAs with higher strength and work hardenability, implying further exploration of this compositional strategy.. Quote: "The addition of Si in DP-5Si-HEA decreased the stability of f.c.c. (γ) matrix thereby promoting pronounced transformation induced plastic deformation"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the Co-Ni balance in a VCrFeCoNi medium-entropy alloy system be tuned to induce an fcc to bcc martensitic transformation for enhancing cryogenic strength-ductility balance?. System: V10Cr10Fe45CoxNi35−x medium-entropy alloys (specifically 10Co, 20Co, 30Co, and 35Co variants). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of pure elements (99.9% purity), homogenization at 1100 °C for 6 hrs, cold-rolling with 75% reduction ratio to 1.5-mm sheets, and annealing at 900 °C for 10 min followed by water-quenching. Test conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature (25 °C) and cryogenic temperature (−196 °C) with a crosshead speed of 6.4 × 10−3 mm·s−1. Findings: The 35Co alloy achieved a cryogenic tensile strength of 1623 MPa, which is twice its room-temperature strength.; At cryogenic temperature, the 35Co alloy exhibited 65% elongation and a yield strength of 653 MPa.; The fraction of fcc phase in the 35Co alloy decreased to 1.1% after cryogenic tensile deformation, indicating extensive fcc to bcc transformation.; The 30Co alloy showed a multiple-stage strain hardening behavior with a hardening rate reaching 3600 MPa in Stage III.; The hcp phase fraction was approximately 5% and acted primarily as a nucleation site for the bcc martensite.; Increasing Co content from 10 to 35 at.% reduced the Gibbs free energy difference (ΔGbcc-fcc) from −1300 to −5800 J·mol−1.; The 35Co alloy displayed a sigmoidal stress-strain curve at cryogenic temperatures, consisting of an easy deformation stage followed by rapid hardening.. Mechanism: The fcc to bcc martensitic transformation generates a complex network structure with high-angle grain boundaries that refines the grain dynamically and introduces large transformation strains, creating mobile dislocations that significantly enhance strain hardening and strength-ductility balance.. Limitations: The authors note that thermodynamic calculations using the database are not accurate below 0 °C, though 0 °C calculations are considered reasonably acceptable for stability evaluation.. Future work: The authors propose that the fcc to bcc transformation can be an attractive route for a new MEA design strategy to improve cryogenic strength-ductility.. Quote: "The Co-Ni balance plays a leading role in phase stability and consequently tunes the cryogenic-temperature strength-ductility balance."
